newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FEATURE - Tough times for Austrian tourism.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Tough times for Austrian tourism.

text.p: Flights to destinations from Africa to Singapore fill the windows of Vienna's travel agents, but while foreign travel blossoms, Austria's own beleaguered tourism industry shows little sign of recovery.

It seems that the delights of the Danube and wonders of the Wienerwald may no longer be enough to keep the tourists flowing into this picturesque Alpine republic, where tough competition and European recessions have hit tourism hard.

Summer season figures (1 May to 31 October) from the Chamber of Economy show that the number of overnight stays, a vital indicator of the strength of the tourism industry, last year fell six percent to 61.8 million from 1995 and registered a 26 percent drop from 78.1 million in 1991.
Austria's economy ministry last month predicted that earnings would continue to deteriorate this summer.

"You can get one week in Austria for the same price as fourteen days in the Caribbean, including the flights," bemoans Professor Walter Ender, tourism expert at the Vienna University of Economics and Business Administration.

"We have to accept that we need to undergo a change from mass tourism to quality tourism," Ender told Reuters. "We cannot influence the social level or the price of aircraft fuel...the only possibility is quality tourism."
Paul Schimka at the Chamber of Economy said the highest expenses were personnel costs. "I can't cut personnel costs much because then the quality is not there anymore," he said.
The Austrian National Tourist Office has undergone a thorough structural overhaul and armed itself with a revised logo and a new slogan: "Austria. Holiday Break Away".
FIGURES SHOW DISTURBING DECLINE
The tourist office's figures reveal a disturbing decline in domestic tourism and visits from Germany and Switzerland, which together account for 75 percent of Austria's tourism.
This does not bode well for a country where tourism last year accounted for six percent of gross domestic product (GDP), down from eight percent in 1995.
Touropa, Austria's biggest holiday company, regularly flies planeloads of tourists to destinations such as Greece, Tunisia, Turkey and the Dominican Republic.
Cycling and hiking are Austria's answer to sun, sea and sand.

Ingrid Krenn, spokeswoman of the state-funded Austrian tourist board, acknowledged that with such tough competition, her task is not easy. She does not see Austrian tourism returning to the highs of five years ago.
"But we are still tourism world masters," she says. "More people go to the Tyrol alone than to Greece and Turkey together...We have to try and be creative and innovative."

In practice, the tourist board's approach puts the emphasis on different Austrian attractions for different countries. For example, it stresses Austrian culture to the Spanish, Alpine pursuits to the German visitor and the classical cliches of Mozart and cosy coffee houses to the Japanese and Americans.

Last year's winter campaign targeted young people with trendy sports like snow-boarding. Austrian tourism advertising appeared on Austrian, German and Swiss television and cinema screens for the first time.
NEED TO EXPLOIT SHORT BREAK MARKET
Krenn points out that package holidays are always more popular with the public.

But the Chamber of Economy's Schimka argues that Austria's tourism industry is not geared to package tours. Instead, he says Austria must exploit the short holiday and niche markets, like culture breaks.
Schimka expects the tourism industry to make a full recovery once the economic situation in Germany improves and the shock of government savings measures in Austria recedes.
Small firms make up 80 percent of Austria's tourism industry, and confronted by complex bureaucracy and accounting procedures, he says.
The German-speaking world remains Austria's core tourist market, but it is Asia, Eastern Europe and the United States that offer most promise for the future.

"The Asian and U.S. markets are expanding constantly," says Josef Bitzinger, in charge of Vienna tourism at the Chamber of Economics. He points to the strong dollar to counter the claim that Austria is still too expensive for many tourists.
Ender notes that more and more airlines are flying to Austria. "With every new airline the number of enquiries from these countries goes up too," he said.
"We have been in Eastern Europe since the beginning, since before the opening (of former Eastern bloc countries)," says Ender.
Tourists from Russia, Hungary and Poland are already in evidence in Vienna, retracing the footsteps of visitors to the Austro-Hungarian empire more than a century ago.
But these new markets may take time to develop.
Until they do, the only sound likely to be enlivening Austria's hills this summer is the distant ring of overhead charter jets, on route to rather more exotic climes.
